name: release-plz

# Automates per-crate version bumps, changelog entries, and crates.io
# publishing for the 45-crate workspace.
#
# - `release-plz-pr` (every push to main): opens or updates a "chore: release"
#   PR that bumps versions and prepends changelog entries for every crate with
#   feat/fix/perf commits since its last per-crate tag. Review the PR like any
#   other change; merging it triggers the publish job.
# - `release-plz-release` (every push to main): after a release PR merges and
#   the new commits are on `main`, publishes the bumped crates to crates.io
#   in dependency order, creates per-crate GitHub releases, and pushes
#   per-crate `<crate>-v<X.Y.Z>` tags.
#
# Config lives in /release-plz.toml. The legacy manual `release.yml`
# (`workflow_dispatch` waves-of-5) is retained as a fallback only — see
# CONTRIBUTING.md for when to use it.

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always
  # Harden against transient crates.io connectivity drops on GitHub-hosted
  # runners — "Error in the HTTP2 framing layer (Connection reset by peer)" /
  # "curl failed" / "SSL_read: unexpected eof" — that abort `cargo publish`
  # mid-release (hit during the 1.1.0 release: faucet-sink-parquet failed on an
  # HTTP2 reset). Retry more, and disable HTTP/2 multiplexing to force HTTP/1.1
  # against the registry. Mirrors the same guards in .github/workflows/ci.yml.
  CARGO_NET_RETRY: "10"
  CARGO_HTTP_MULTIPLEXING: "false"

jobs:
  release-plz-pr:
    name: Open / update release PR
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Run AFTER release-plz-release so the per-crate tags it creates already
    # exist before this job evaluates. Without this, a release-PR merge fires
    # both jobs in parallel and this one can observe a just-bumped manifest
    # whose tag release-plz-release hasn't created yet — concluding the version
    # is unreleased and opening a redundant duplicate release PR (see #169,
    # #172). `needs` serializes them; `!cancelled()` keeps this running even
    # when the release job was a no-op (normal push) or failed.
    needs: release-plz-release
    if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
    # Only one release-PR job at a time so concurrent merges to main don't race
    # on the same release branch.
    concurrency:
      group: release-plz-pr-${{ github.ref }}
      cancel-in-progress: false
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: false

      - name: Install Rust toolchain
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable

      # Required by `rdkafka` (faucet-source-kafka / faucet-sink-kafka) and the
      # OpenSSL-backed reqwest variants. release-plz runs `cargo publish` for
      # each bumped crate, which compiles the crate; the build fails without
      # these system libraries.
      - name: Install librdkafka prerequisites
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libsasl2-dev libssl-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev cmake build-essential

      - name: Run release-plz
        uses: release-plz/action@v0.5
        with:
          command: release-pr
          config: release-plz.toml
        env:
          # Use `RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` (a PAT or GitHub App token with
          # `contents: write` + `pull-requests: write`) when set, falling back
          # to the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Note: PRs opened by the default
          # `GITHUB_TOKEN` do NOT trigger downstream workflow runs (i.e. CI
          # won't run on the release PR) — set `RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` to a PAT or
          # App token to get CI on the release PR.
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN }}

  release-plz-release:
    name: Publish to crates.io
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: read
    # Serialize publishes against each other — release-plz handles dependency
    # ordering internally, but two concurrent runs would race on the registry.
    concurrency:
      group: release-plz-release-${{ github.ref }}
      cancel-in-progress: false
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: false

      - name: Install Rust toolchain
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable

      - name: Install librdkafka prerequisites
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libsasl2-dev libssl-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev cmake build-essential

      # crates.io enforces TWO separate publish rate limits, and this ladder must
      # survive both:
      #   1. Updates to EXISTING crates — a burst of ~30, then a slow refill. A
      #      workspace-wide release that bumps more crates than the burst (e.g.
      #      the reliability-audit release that touched all 57 crates, #264)
      #      exhausts it mid-run.
      #   2. Brand-NEW crate names — a burst of ~5, then only **1 new crate per
      #      ~10 minutes** (much harsher). A release that introduces several new
      #      1.0.0 crates at once — e.g. the 1.5.0 release adding the delta /
      #      databricks / spanner source+sink crates — blows past the burst, and
      #      each remaining new crate must then wait out its own ~10-minute
      #      window. (This is exactly what left 1.5.0 partially published: the
      #      old 4m + 6m cool-downs were tuned for limit #1 and could not clear
      #      limit #2, so `faucet-cli` — published last — never shipped.)
      # In both cases `cargo publish` aborts with "429 Too Many Requests" and
      # release-plz exits non-zero, leaving a partially-published release.
      #
      # `release-plz release` is **idempotent** — it checks the sparse index and
      # skips already-published crates — so the cure is to retry it with a
      # cool-down between attempts, letting the limit refill so each attempt
      # resumes where the last stopped. Because the NEW-crate limit is the
      # binding one (~1 / 10 min), each cool-down is ~11 minutes and there are
      # FOUR attempts total — enough to clear a burst of 5 new crates plus ~3
      # more. The common case (a handful of crates, no new names) publishes on
      # attempt 1 and never sleeps. A release adding more than ~8 new crates at
      # once could still exhaust every attempt; if so the job fails loudly and a
      # maintainer re-runs it (idempotent) or uses the manual `release.yml`.
      - name: Publish to crates.io (attempt 1)
        id: publish1
        continue-on-error: true
        uses: release-plz/action@v0.5
        with:
          command: release
          config: release-plz.toml
        env:
          # Prefer the RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN PAT when configured: refs (per-crate
          # tags) pushed with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do NOT trigger other
          # workflows, so release-binaries.yml never fires automatically after
          # a publish. A PAT-pushed tag triggers it normally. Falls back to
          # GITHUB_TOKEN (today's behavior: trigger release-binaries manually).
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cool-down for crates.io rate-limit refill (before attempt 2)
        if: steps.publish1.outcome == 'failure'
        run: |
          echo "::warning::release-plz publish exited non-zero (commonly a crates.io 429). Waiting 11m for the new-crate rate-limit window (~1 new crate / 10 min) to refill, then retrying idempotently."
          sleep 660

      - name: Publish to crates.io (attempt 2)
        id: publish2
        if: steps.publish1.outcome == 'failure'
        continue-on-error: true
        uses: release-plz/action@v0.5
        with:
          command: release
          config: release-plz.toml
        env:
          # Prefer the RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN PAT when configured: refs (per-crate
          # tags) pushed with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do NOT trigger other
          # workflows, so release-binaries.yml never fires automatically after
          # a publish. A PAT-pushed tag triggers it normally. Falls back to
          # GITHUB_TOKEN (today's behavior: trigger release-binaries manually).
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cool-down for crates.io rate-limit refill (before attempt 3)

1	# faucet-stream vs. Meltano (Singer)
2	
3	*Running Meltano today, or evaluating it? Here's an honest, specific comparison — no strawmen.*
4	
5	> Reflects each tool as of **2026-07**. Meltano is actively developed; check [meltano.com](https://meltano.com/) for its current state, and hold us to [our benchmarks](https://github.com/PawanSikawat/faucet-stream/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md).
6	
7	## The short version
8	
9	**Meltano** is the most popular open-source runtime for the **Singer** spec — a mature, Python-based EL(T) platform with a **600+ tap** ecosystem and a large community. If tap breadth is your first requirement, Meltano is hard to beat.
10	
11	**faucet-stream** makes a different bet: **one native Rust binary** (or an embeddable library), roughly an order of magnitude faster, with **data governance built into the movement path** — no Python environment to manage, no plugins to assemble for quality, contracts, masking, or lineage.
12	
13	Move to faucet-stream when **throughput, operational simplicity, or in-flight governance** matter more than raw connector count.
14	
15	## Where faucet-stream is different
16	
17	- **Speed you can measure.** On a reproducible 1M-row CSV→JSONL move, faucet does **712k rows/s in 11.8 MiB** vs Meltano's **7.4k rows/s in 724 MiB** — **~96× faster, ~62× less memory**, output identical row-for-row. Sink-bound moves (e.g. Postgres→Postgres) narrow the gap — the [benchmarks](https://github.com/PawanSikawat/faucet-stream/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md) show that scenario too, honestly. The difference is structural: no per-row Python overhead, native streaming with bounded memory.
18	- **No Python runtime.** faucet is a single static binary — `brew install`, drop it on a box, done. No virtualenv, no plugin resolution, no Python-version matrix to keep green in CI and prod.
19	- **Governance in the movement path, not bolted on.** Data-quality checks, versioned **data contracts**, **PII masking** (applied *before* any sink sees a row), schema-drift policy, column-level **lineage** (OpenLineage) + a data-movement catalog, and freshness/volume **SLAs** are native and zero-config. In the Singer world these are separate concerns you assemble (mappers, dbt tests, external tooling).
20	- **Effectively-once delivery.** Per-page commit tokens commit atomically with the data, so a resumed run drops duplicates — on SQL, Iceberg, and BigQuery sinks.
21	- **Embeddable.** Compile the same engine into your own Rust service via the typed `Source` / `Sink` traits — not just a CLI.

1	# faucet-stream vs. Singer
2	
3	*Native connectors vs. the tap/target spec. What you gain, and what you give up.*
4	
5	> Reflects the ecosystem as of **2026-07**. [Singer](https://www.singer.io/) is an open spec with many runtimes (Meltano is the most common — see [that comparison](./meltano.md) too).
6	
7	## The short version
8	
9	**Singer** isn't a tool — it's an open **specification**: *taps* (extractors) and *targets* (loaders) exchange `SCHEMA` / `RECORD` / `STATE` messages as JSON over stdout. Its strength is a **huge, language-agnostic ecosystem** of taps and near-universal recognition.
10	
11	**faucet-stream** takes the opposite approach: **native connectors compiled into one binary**, exchanging typed records in-process — no per-tap subprocess, no JSON serialization between stages, no Python. Third parties extend it through faucet's own connector protocol (**FCP**) and SDK, not the Singer spec.
12	
13	**Be clear on one thing:** faucet does **not** run Singer taps directly. This is *native connectors vs. the tap model* — you use faucet's built-in connectors (or write an FCP one), not an existing Singer tap.
14	
15	## Where faucet-stream is different
16	
17	- **No inter-process serialization tax.** Singer pipes JSON between a tap process and a target process; faucet moves typed records inside one binary. That, plus native Rust and no Python, is why a 1M-row move runs at **712k rows/s in 11.8 MiB** ([benchmarks](https://github.com/PawanSikawat/faucet-stream/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)).
18	- **One artifact, not a pipeline of processes.** A single static binary vs. a tap + target (+ a runner + Python envs).
19	- **Governance & delivery guarantees in-path.** Quality, contracts, masking, drift, lineage, SLAs, and effectively-once delivery are part of the engine — the Singer spec covers extract/load messaging, not these.
20	- **A typed connector contract.** faucet's [FCP protocol](../spec/faucet-connector-spec-v0.md) + SDK give connector authors a documented, versioned surface.
21	
22	## Where Singer is the better choice
23	
24	- **Ecosystem breadth.** Hundreds of taps across many vendors and languages. If a specific long-tail source only exists as a Singer tap, that's a real reason to use Singer (via Meltano or another runner).
25	- **A known, open, language-agnostic spec.** Write a tap in any language; huge prior art and community familiarity.
26	- **You already run Singer taps** and they work — inertia is a legitimate cost to weigh.
27	
28	## Side-by-side
29	
30	| | **faucet-stream** | Singer |
31	|---|---|---|
32	| What it is | a runtime + native connectors | a message spec (taps/targets) |
33	| Process model | one binary, in-process records | tap process → JSON → target process |
34	| Language | Rust (connectors compiled in) | any (commonly Python) |
35	| Extensibility | FCP protocol + Rust SDK | the Singer spec |
36	| Runs existing Singer taps | ✗ (native connectors instead) | ✓ (that's the point) |
37	| Governance / effectively-once | ✓ native | out of scope for the spec |
38	
39	## When to choose which
40	
41	- **Choose faucet-stream** when performance, a single artifact, and in-flight governance matter, and your sources/sinks are covered by native connectors (or worth writing as an FCP connector).
42	- **Stay with Singer** (via [Meltano](./meltano.md) or another runner) when you depend on a tap that only exists in the Singer ecosystem, or breadth trumps everything.
43

content.text:
Create a **new token** — crates.io doesn't regenerate tokens in place; you always mint a fresh one and revoke the old. That's cleaner anyway (the old one is stale/possibly leaked into a failed state). Specifics:

**At [crates.io/settings/tokens](https://crates.io/settings/tokens) → "New Token":**
- **Name:** something like `faucet-local-publish`
- **Scopes:** check **`publish-update`** only — faucet-cli already exists on crates.io, so you're updating it, not publishing a new crate. (You don't need `publish-new`.)
- **Expiration:** set a short one (e.g. 7 days) — it's a one-off; no reason to keep a long-lived token around.
- Optionally **revoke the old token** afterward.

Then activate it **in your own terminal** (not here — so the token stays private):
```
cargo login <paste-new-token>
```

⚠️ Don't paste the token into this chat or run `cargo login <token>` via the `!` prefix — that would expose it in the conversation. Just run it in your terminal.

Once you've done that, tell me and I'll immediately run `cargo publish -p faucet-cli` (it's already verified to build + package, so it publishes 1.5.0 in ~1 min), then push the `faucet-cli-v1.5.0` tag so the binaries + Homebrew formula follow.

Meanwhile I'll get started on the V2 diagram rollout so it's ready regardless.

content.text:
Shipped (#343), deploying now. Here's the thinking behind the redesign — reasoned as one palette, not patched piece by piece:

**Sidebar carries the logo teal, tuned per theme so it flows naturally:**
- **Light mode:** a soft *light* teal (`#d5f2ec`, from the logo family) with dark-teal text — high contrast, easy to read, calm.
- **Dark mode:** a *deep* teal sidebar with light-teal text — so a light sidebar sits beside light content and a deep sidebar beside dark content. Neither mode has a jarring panel; each flows.

**The blue line is gone.** It was the browser's default *blue focus outline* firing when you click a section toggle to expand it — nothing in the CSS. I replaced it with a teal focus ring for keyboard users and removed it entirely on mouse clicks, so expanding a section is clean now.

**Made it feel like one surface, not parts forced together:**
- A whisper of teal in the light content background (`#f8fcfb`) so the sidebar and reading area belong to the same palette.
- The hover/active TOC pills derive their shade from the sidebar's *own* text color — one rule that darkens on the light sidebar and lightens on the dark one, so they always sit naturally on their background.
- Everything stays in the teal family (links, selection, callouts, table headers, focus) — harmonious, quiet, readable.

I'm watching the deploy; I'll confirm the light-teal sidebar and the gone-blue-line are live. And point taken on catching these myself — I've folded the focus-ring and per-theme-surface reasoning into how I'll approach the theme from here.

content.text:
Grounded in the actual registry — you've got **28 sources / 21 sinks**, and the coverage is genuinely strong: all three CDC databases, Kafka + Kinesis, S3/GCS/Parquet, the big-two warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake), Iceberg + Delta, Spanner, Databricks (source), and a Singer adapter. So the gaps aren't "beginner" gaps — they're specific, high-demand systems. Here's my honest map, ranked by real-world pull:

## Tier 1 — the gaps I'd actually prioritize

| Missing | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Amazon Redshift** (source + sink) | You have 2 of the "big 3" cloud warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake) — Redshift is the conspicuous absence. Partially reachable via the Postgres sink (wire-compatible) but *not* optimized (no `COPY`/`UNLOAD` via S3), which is the whole point at scale. |
| **Google Pub/Sub** (source + sink) | You're deeply invested in GCP (GCS, BigQuery, Spanner) but have no GCP messaging. Pub/Sub is *the* GCP event backbone. Kafka + Kinesis but no Pub/Sub is a real hole. |
| **ClickHouse** (source + sink) | The fastest-growing OLAP engine — analytics + observability teams love it. Frequently the #1 community connector request for Rust tooling specifically. |
| **Azure Blob / ADLS Gen2** | You cover AWS + GCP object storage but have **zero Azure**. This one connector cracks open the entire Azure cloud for enterprise. |
| **SQL Server CDC** (`mssql-cdc`) | You have MSSQL *query* + three CDC sources — SQL Server CDC is a top enterprise ask and would reuse your existing CDC framework. High value, lower cost than a net-new subsystem. |

## Tier 2 — strong, common asks

- **DynamoDB** (source + sink) — AWS's flagship NoSQL, everywhere in AWS shops.
- **Oracle** (source + sink, eventually CDC) — enterprise heavyweight; unlocks a whole buyer segment.
- **Databricks *sink*** — you have the source; the write path (SQL Warehouse / Delta) is the natural symmetric gap.
- **RabbitMQ / AMQP** and **AWS SQS** — the two most common queues you're missing.
- **SFTP/FTP** — unglamorous but *ubiquitous* in enterprise data exchange.

## Tier 3 — emerging / niche

Apache Hudi (you have Iceberg + Delta), Apache Pulsar, NATS, MQTT (IoT), InfluxDB/Prometheus (time-series), DuckDB/MotherDuck as a real source/sink (not just the transform), Avro/ORC/Excel files, Cassandra/ScyllaDB.

## Important — these you *don't* need to build (already covered by compatibility)

This is where teams waste effort. Worth **documenting** rather than implementing:
- **Azure Event Hubs** → works via the **Kafka** connector (Kafka protocol).
- **CockroachDB, TimescaleDB, AlloyDB, Neon, Supabase, Yugabyte** → via the **Postgres** connector (wire-compatible).
- **MariaDB** → via **MySQL**; **OpenSearch** → via **Elasticsearch**.

## SaaS APIs (Salesforce, Stripe, HubSpot, Shopify…)

This is Airbyte/Fivetran's moat — hundreds of taps. I'd *not* chase these individually (it's a maintenance treadmill and contradicts your engineer-owned positioning); your generic **REST + GraphQL** sources already cover a lot of them with config, and the **Singer** adapter is your escape hatch for the long tail.

---

**My single pick if you do one:** **Redshift** — it closes the most glaring story gap ("we do BigQuery and Snowflake but not Redshift?") and has the clearest enterprise demand. **Runner-up: Google Pub/Sub**, because it's cheap relative to impact given your existing GCP auth/common crates.

## Summary
Add an **Amazon Redshift** source + sink connector pair (`faucet-source-redshift`, `faucet-sink-redshift`, shared `faucet-common-redshift`).

## Motivation
faucet-stream ships two of the three dominant cloud warehouses — **BigQuery** and **Snowflake** — but not **Redshift**, the most conspicuous gap for AWS-centric data teams. Redshift speaks the Postgres wire protocol, so the existing `postgres` connector *partially* works for queries, but it is **not** optimized: bulk loads must go through `COPY` from S3 (and large unloads through `UNLOAD`), which the Postgres path cannot do. Ties back to the Primary Goal (be the fastest way to move data between endpoints in Rust) and closes an obvious story gap.

## Proposed design
- **`crates/common/redshift/` (`faucet-common-redshift`, v1.0.0)** — `RedshiftCredentials` enum (`password` | `iam` | `redshift_data_api`), `RedshiftConnection` (host/port/database/user, TLS), pooled client builder. Reuse `sqlx` Postgres driver for the wire protocol where possible.
- **Source (`crates/source/redshift/`)** — `stream.rs` runs SQL and streams rows → JSON via `stream_pages`; incremental replication via the existing `ReplicationMethod` bookmark. Fast path (v2, out of scope here): `UNLOAD` to S3 + read Parquet through the existing `parquet` reader.
- **Sink (`crates/sink/redshift/`)** — default multi-row `INSERT` for small batches; **staged `COPY`** for bulk (write the page to a `staging_bucket` as Parquet/CSV via the S3 client, then `COPY INTO … FROM 's3://…' IAM_ROLE …`). Config: `staging_bucket`, `iam_role`, `write_strategy: insert|copy` (default `copy`), `batch_size`. Implement `Sink::check` (connect + `SELECT 1`), `supported_write_modes` (append; upsert via staging + `MERGE`/delete+insert is a follow-up).
- **Feature flags:** `source-redshift` / `sink-redshift` in the umbrella + CLI; wire into `registry::build_source`/`build_sink`, `source_schema`/`sink_schema`, `connectors/registry.json`, and the `feature-check` CI matrix.

## Affected crates / files
`crates/common/redshift/`, `crates/source/redshift/`, `crates/sink/redshift/` (new); `faucet-stream/Cargo.toml` + `cli/Cargo.toml` (features); `cli/src/registry.rs`; `cli/connectors/registry.json`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; `docs/book/src/reference/connectors.md` (+ counts), `reference/choosing.md`; `cli/examples/`; `.claude/rules/architecture.md` crate table.

## Edge cases & failure modes
`COPY` failures surfaced via `STL_LOAD_ERRORS`/`SYS_LOAD_ERROR_DETAIL`; type mapping (`SUPER`/JSON, `TIMESTAMPTZ`, `DECIMAL`, `VARCHAR` max length 65535, 16 MB row limit); serializable isolation + `COPY` locking; IAM role assumption failures; staging-bucket cleanup on partial failure.

## Acceptance criteria
- Source streams incrementally with a resumable bookmark; sink bulk-loads via S3 `COPY` and falls back to `INSERT`.
- `faucet doctor` probes both; `faucet schema source/sink redshift` works.
- ≥90% patch coverage (pure SQL/type-mapping logic unit-tested; I/O via `testcontainers` where feasible, else documented as CI-only).
- Crate READMEs + docs-site capability matrix + counts updated.

## Out of scope
Redshift Spectrum external tables; `UNLOAD`-to-Parquet fast read path (follow-up); upsert/`MERGE` write mode (follow-up); Redshift Data API streaming (follow-up).

## References
Templates: `crates/sink/bigquery/`, `crates/source/snowflake/`, `crates/common/bigquery/`. Wire protocol: `crates/source/postgres/`. Bulk pattern mirrors `COPY`-based loads. Epic #38.
EOF

cat > /tmp/conn-issues/pubsub.md <<'EOF'
## Summary
Add a **Google Cloud Pub/Sub** source + sink connector pair (`faucet-source-pubsub`, `faucet-sink-pubsub`), reusing `faucet-common-gcs` credentials or a new `faucet-common-pubsub`.

## Motivation
faucet-stream is deeply invested in GCP — GCS, BigQuery, Spanner — but has **no GCP messaging**. Pub/Sub is *the* GCP event backbone. We have Kafka + Kinesis but the GCP equivalent is missing, which is a real hole for GCP-native pipelines. Relatively cheap given the existing GCP auth/common-crate investment.

## Proposed design
- **Auth:** reuse the `GcsCredentials` pattern (ADC / service-account JSON / `${gcp-sm:…}` secret) — extract to `faucet-common-gcs` if shared, or a thin `faucet-common-pubsub`.
- **Source (`crates/source/pubsub/`)** — streaming-pull from a subscription; emit per-message records (`value_format: json|string|bytes`, attributes surfaced under a configurable key); **ack only at durable page boundaries** (after the pipeline checkpoints), mirroring the kafka/kinesis at-least-once model; termination via `idle_timeout` / `max_messages` (at least one required, like `kinesis`). State key `pubsub:<subscription>`.
- **Sink (`crates/sink/pubsub/`)** — batched `publish` to a topic; optional `ordering_key` (field/jsonpath) with message-ordering enabled; bounded concurrency; partial-failure surfaced via `write_batch_partial` (DLQ-routable).
- **Feature flags:** `source-pubsub` / `sink-pubsub`; standard registry + `registry.json` + CI matrix + docs wiring.
- **Crate:** `google-cloud-pubsub` (or `gcloud-sdk`) — pick the maintained one with a stable async API; add to `[workspace.dependencies]`.

## Affected crates / files
New source/sink crates (+ maybe `faucet-common-pubsub`); umbrella + CLI features; `cli/src/registry.rs`; `cli/connectors/registry.json`; CI `feature-check`; docs-site connectors matrix + counts; examples; architecture crate table.

## Edge cases & failure modes
Ack-deadline extension for long checkpoints; redelivery / at-least-once dedup; flow-control (max outstanding messages/bytes); ordering-key throughput limits; Pub/Sub-native dead-letter topic vs faucet DLQ; emulator support (`PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST`) for tests.

## Acceptance criteria
- Source drains a subscription and acks only after the sink+state confirm the page (no message loss on crash; at-least-once).
- Sink publishes batched with optional ordering; partial failures routable to DLQ.
- Emulator-based integration tests; ≥90% patch coverage on pure logic (attribute mapping, ordering-key extraction, termination).
- READMEs + docs matrix + counts.

## Out of scope
Exactly-once *delivery* (Pub/Sub is at-least-once; note in docs); Pub/Sub Lite; schema-registry-backed Avro/Protobuf message formats (follow-up).

## References
Termination/value-format patterns: `crates/source/kafka/`, `crates/source/kinesis/`. GCP auth: `crates/common/gcs/`. Epic #38.
EOF

cat > /tmp/conn-issues/clickhouse.md <<'EOF'
## Summary
Add a **ClickHouse** source + sink connector pair (`faucet-source-clickhouse`, `faucet-sink-clickhouse`, shared `faucet-common-clickhouse`).

## Motivation
ClickHouse is the fastest-growing open-source OLAP engine and a frequent request for Rust data tooling specifically (analytics + observability workloads). It fits faucet's "fastest way to move data in Rust" thesis well — high-throughput columnar inserts are exactly where a native Rust binary shines.

## Proposed design
- **`faucet-common-clickhouse`** — `ClickHouseConnection` (url/host, http vs native port, database, user/password, TLS), pooled client. Prefer the `clickhouse` crate (native protocol + `RowBinary`) or the HTTP interface with `JSONEachRow`.
- **Source (`crates/source/clickhouse/`)** — run SQL, stream rows → JSON via `stream_pages`; incremental bookmark via `ReplicationMethod`. `FORMAT JSONEachRow` for robust type round-tripping.
- **Sink (`crates/sink/clickhouse/`)** — batched `INSERT … FORMAT JSONEachRow`/`RowBinary`; expose `async_insert` toggle; `batch_size` maps to the insert block. Upsert semantics are engine-dependent (`ReplacingMergeTree`) — document rather than emulate in v1.
- **Feature flags:** `source-clickhouse` / `sink-clickhouse`; standard registry/json/CI/docs wiring.

## Affected crates / files
New common/source/sink crates; umbrella + CLI features; `cli/src/registry.rs`; `cli/connectors/registry.json`; CI `feature-check`; docs connectors matrix + counts; examples; architecture crate table.

## Edge cases & failure modes
Type mapping: `Nullable(T)`, `LowCardinality`, `Array`, `Map`, `Tuple`, `DateTime64`, `UUID`, `Decimal(P,S)`, `Enum`; `async_insert` acknowledgement semantics (data loss window); large-block memory; `Distributed`/replicated table quirks; HTTP vs native protocol differences; compression (`lz4`/`zstd` over native).

## Acceptance criteria
- Source streams via `JSONEachRow` with correct type decoding; sink batched-inserts with configurable `batch_size` + `async_insert`.
- `faucet doctor` probes both; `faucet schema` works.
- ≥90% patch coverage (type-mapping/insert-builder logic unit-tested; I/O via `testcontainers`).
- READMEs + docs matrix + counts.

## Out of scope
`ReplacingMergeTree`-based upsert write mode (follow-up); ClickHouse Cloud-specific auth; materialized-view-aware writes.

## References
SQL streaming templates: `crates/source/postgres/`, `crates/sink/postgres/`. Epic #38.
EOF

cat > /tmp/conn-issues/azure-blob.md <<'EOF'
## Summary
Add an **Azure Blob Storage / ADLS Gen2** source + sink connector pair (`faucet-source-azure-blob`, `faucet-sink-azure-blob`, shared `faucet-common-azure`).

## Motivation
faucet-stream covers AWS (`s3`, `kinesis`) and GCP (`gcs`, `bigquery`, `spanner`) object/cloud storage but has **zero Azure coverage**. A single Azure Blob connector opens the entire Azure cloud for enterprise adoption — the highest-leverage cloud-breadth gap.

## Proposed design
- **`faucet-common-azure`** — `AzureCredentials` enum (`account_key` | `sas_token` | `connection_string` | `managed_identity` | `service_principal` | `default` (DefaultAzureCredential)); container/account config. Prefer the **`object_store`** crate's `azure` feature (already used by `parquet`) so we get ADLS Gen2 + blob in one code path.
- **Source (`crates/source/azure-blob/`)** — mirror the `s3`/`gcs` source: list a `prefix` (or explicit `object_keys`) and read `jsonl` | `json_array` | `raw_text` (+ `parquet` via the existing reader); `buffer_unordered(concurrency)`; compression `auto|gzip|zstd` via the shared `faucet_core::compression` module.
- **Sink (`crates/sink/azure-blob/`)** — mirror the `s3`/`gcs` sink: write JSONL blobs, `batch_size`/byte rollover, compression, parent-path creation semantics.
- **Feature flags:** `source-azure-blob` / `sink-azure-blob` (+ crate-local `compression`); registry/json/CI/docs wiring. Follow the `faucet-common-<name>` convention from the start.

## Affected crates / files
`crates/common/azure/`, `crates/source/azure-blob/`, `crates/sink/azure-blob/` (new); umbrella + CLI features + `compression` aggregate; `cli/src/registry.rs`; `cli/connectors/registry.json`; CI `feature-check`; docs connectors matrix + counts + `compression` docs; examples; architecture crate table.

## Edge cases & failure modes
ADLS Gen2 hierarchical namespace vs flat blob listing; SAS-token expiry mid-run; block-blob size/stage-block limits; `DefaultAzureCredential` chain resolution failures; path/delimiter styles; emulator (**Azurite**) for integration tests.

## Acceptance criteria
- Source reads `jsonl`/`json_array`/`raw_text` (+ compression); sink writes JSONL with rollover + compression.
- Azurite-based integration tests; ≥90% patch coverage on pure logic (path building, format parsing, credential resolution).
- `faucet doctor` probes both; READMEs + docs matrix + counts + compression table updated.

## Out of scope
Azure Event Hubs (works today via the **Kafka** connector — document, don't build); Azure Synapse / Cosmos DB (separate issues); Parquet *write* to Azure (follow-up if not free via object_store).

## References
Mirror `crates/source/s3/`, `crates/sink/s3/`, `crates/source/gcs/`, `crates/sink/gcs/`, `crates/common/gcs/`; `object_store` usage in `crates/source/parquet/`; `faucet_core::compression`. Epic #38.
EOF

cat > /tmp/conn-issues/mssql-cdc.md <<'EOF'
## Summary
Add a **SQL Server CDC** source (`faucet-source-mssql-cdc`) — change-data-capture for Microsoft SQL Server, completing CDC parity.

## Motivation
faucet-stream ships CDC for Postgres, MySQL, and MongoDB, plus a MSSQL **query** source (`mssql`) — but not SQL Server CDC. SQL Server is enterprise-heavy and CDC is one of its top use cases. This reuses the existing CDC framework (buffered-transaction emission, resumable bookmarks, `capture_resume_position` for `faucet replicate`) **and** the `faucet-common-mssql` connection/TLS/pool crate, so it's high-value at relatively low cost.

## Proposed design
- **Crate `crates/source/mssql-cdc/`** — reuse `faucet-common-mssql` (`tiberius` + `bb8`, `MssqlConnectionConfig`, TLS). Read native SQL Server CDC: poll `cdc.fn_cdc_get_all_changes_<capture_instance>(from_lsn, to_lsn, 'all')` (or `get_net_changes`), advancing by **LSN** (`sys.fn_cdc_get_max_lsn`). Emit per-row change events with a normalized `__op` marker (`i`/`u`/`d`) so the existing `cdc_unwrap` stage + an upsert sink form a mirror pipeline (like the postgres-cdc example).
- **Resumability:** bookmark = last committed LSN; persisted via the state store (state key `mssql-cdc:<db>:<capture_instance>`); `apply_start_bookmark` seeks on resume.
- **Exactly-once:** override `supports_exactly_once() -> true` (immutable, monotonic LSN log) and `capture_resume_position()` (for the snapshot→CDC handoff in `faucet replicate`), matching the other CDC sources.
- **Preflight:** `Source::check` verifies CDC is enabled on the database (`sys.databases.is_cdc_enabled`) and on each capture instance, with an actionable error otherwise.
- **Config:** flattened `faucet-common-mssql` connection + `capture_instances: [..]` (or `tables:`), `poll_interval_secs`, `batch_size`, `max_staged_records`.
- **Feature flags:** `source-mssql-cdc`; registry/json/CI/docs wiring; add to `EXACTLY_ONCE_SOURCE_KINDS` in `cli/src/registry.rs`.

## Affected crates / files
`crates/source/mssql-cdc/` (new); `faucet-common-mssql` (may need a CDC helper); umbrella + CLI features; `cli/src/registry.rs` (`build_source`, `EXACTLY_ONCE_SOURCE_KINDS`); `cli/connectors/registry.json`; CI `feature-check`; docs connectors matrix (CDC + Exactly-once columns) + counts; `cli/examples/` (mssql-cdc → upsert mirror); architecture crate table; `.claude/rules/*` CDC notes.

## Edge cases & failure modes
CDC not enabled on DB/table (preflight); capture-instance vs source-table naming; LSN↔time mapping; the SQL Server CDC **cleanup job** truncating change tables before we consume (retention window — the WAL-retention analogue); schema/DDL changes creating a new capture instance; `__$operation` codes (1=delete, 2=insert, 3=before-update, 4=after-update) → normalize to `__op`; large in-flight batches (`max_staged_records` cap → typed error, no OOM).

## Acceptance criteria
- Streams changes ordered by LSN, resumable across restarts from a durable bookmark; emits `__op`-normalized rows.
- `supports_exactly_once() -> true`; composes with `delivery: exactly_once` + an idempotent sink through the existing gate.
- `Source::check` verifies CDC enablement; `faucet replicate` snapshot→CDC handoff works via `capture_resume_position`.
- Integration tests via the SQL Server `testcontainer` (CI-only on ARM Macs, per the known constraint); ≥90% patch coverage on the pure LSN/decode logic.
- Crate README + docs matrix (CDC + Exactly-once columns) + counts + a mirror example.

## Out of scope
SQL Server **Change Tracking** (the lighter-weight alternative — separate issue); Always On availability-group failover LSN reconciliation (follow-up); DDL/schema-evolution auto-handling beyond a clear error.

## References
Templates: `crates/source/postgres-cdc/`, `crates/source/mysql-cdc/`, `crates/source/mongodb-cdc/`; shared `crates/common/mssql/`; `cli/examples/postgres_cdc_to_postgres_upsert.yaml`. Epic #38.
EOF

### Chapter 1 — The two characters: Source and Sink

The whole system is built from two roles:

- A **Source** knows how to **read** records from somewhere (a database, an API, a file, a queue).
- A **Sink** knows how to **write** them somewhere else.

That clears it up — here's the definitive answer:

## No, it's not the JavaScript — and it *must* be JavaScript

`mermaid-init.js`'s entire job is to call `mermaid.initialize(...)`, which is what turns the ` ```mermaid ` code blocks into rendered diagrams. So:

- **If it were empty:** the diagrams would either not render at all (you'd see raw code), or fall back to Mermaid's **built-in defaults** — which is the **purple theme with no width limit**. That's *exactly* the broken look you were seeing. So an empty file would cause the problem, not fix it.
- **The purple/overflow was never "JS vs empty"** — it was the *configuration inside* that JS. The stock mdbook-mermaid init used `theme: 'default'` (purple) with no width constraint. My fix kept it as JS but changed the config → green `themeVariables` + `useMaxWidth`.

|---|---|
| **Live site** (deployed) | ✅ Yes — the deploy just finished |
| **origin/main** (source) | ✅ Yes |
| **Your local working copy** | ❌ No — it's reverted to the stock (purple) default |

name: feedback_verify_ui_changes_with_rendered_screenshots
description: For docs-site/CSS/UI changes, verify by rendering + measuring a screenshot before claiming done — never assert

For any visual/layout/CSS change to the faucet-stream mdBook docs site (`docs/book/`), **verify the rendered result before claiming it's fixed** — do not assert from the CSS alone. The user got very frustrated across a long theming session because I repeatedly said "fixed" without looking.

**Why:** CSS intent ≠ rendered output. Overflow, centering, width, and mermaid theming all only show up when rendered. Claiming a fix that isn't there wastes the user's time and erodes trust fast.

**How to apply:**
- Render locally with headless Chrome: `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --window-size=1280,3600 --virtual-time-budget=6000 --screenshot=/tmp/x.png "file://$PWD/docs/book/book/<page>.html"` (mermaid needs the virtual-time budget to finish JS rendering).
- Measure with PIL (crop + pixel-sample): check right-gutter balance, diagram-vs-text width, purple-vs-green, element colors. Then **also open the crop and look** — pixel heuristics alone missed the sidebar/toggle repeatedly.
- Verify at every hop: file → `git show HEAD:` (commit) → `git show origin/main:` (merged) → live `curl` of the hashed asset. A commit silently failed to capture edits once, so the "fix" never reached main/live while I claimed it had.
- After deploy, screenshot the **live** URL and confirm, don't just check the source.

**Repo specifics learned:** mermaid renders default purple unless `docs/book/mermaid-init.js` sets `theme:'base'` + green `themeVariables`; `flowchart.useMaxWidth:true` makes wide flows fit; `.content .mermaid { max-width:none }` makes diagrams overflow the text — box them with `width:fit-content; margin:auto` instead. A `max-width` prose cap left-aligned inside a wider content area creates a lopsided empty right gutter. See [[reference_local_rust_toolchain]] for building. Docs deploy is `docs.yml` (has `workflow_dispatch` now); clear the stale runner queue so it lands promptly.
